1. To harmonise development efforts and to ensure programmatic coherence and mutual 
reinforcement under the umbrella of the United Nations System-wide Special Initiative on Africa the 
United Nations system in Kenya has prepared the United Nations Development Assistance Framework 
(UNDAF). The purpose of the UNDAF is to orient. rationalise, and encourage increased 
programmatic collaboration by coordinating the contributions of the various United Nations agencies 
toward the achievement of the United Nations mission, given each Agency's mandate and decisionrnaking proccsscs. The UNDAF is the principal country leve! expression of global United Nations 
reform efforts to optimise goal-oriented development cooperation in support of Kenya· s economic and 
social development. 
2. The United Nations system in Kenya is comprised of United Nations Development Group 
members (UNDP. UNICEF. UNFPA, WFP, UNOCP, UNCHS, UNOPS, UNIFEM and UNAIDS). 
other United Nations Funds and Programmes (UNHCR. UNSO/UNDP. UNOCHA, UNON. UNIC) 
and Uníted Natíons Specialized Agencies (ICAO, UNEP, WHO, UNESCO, FAO and UNIDO). The 
representatives of Uníted Nations agencies constitute the United Nations Kenya Country Committee 
(KCC) which is guided by the mission, principies and collaborative modalities established under the 
UNDAF. Bretton Woods lnstitutions (WB, IMF and IFC) also participate as partners in the KCC and 
assisted with the development of the UNDAF for Kenya. 
3. UNDAF/Kenya is based on the overriding development challenges faced by Kenya that have 
been identified in the Govemment of Kenya's Country Strategy Note (CSN) of 1994, the Eighth 
National Development Plan (1997), the United Nations Common Country Assessment (CCA), United 
Nations global conference declarations and platforms for action, United Nations conventions and 
outreach with development panners. The Govemment of Kenya (GoK) has outlined it's strategies in 
various sessional and policy framework papers which cover a broad range of interventions on national 
development issues. 
➔. The United Nations recognises that the Govemment of Kenya retains a sectoral approach to 
programme development. Adopting the programme approach. the United Nations. through lJNDAF. 
will be able to work jointly with Govemment to develop clear and measurable outputs and indicators 
for improved plans of action. 
5. To respond to national priorities during the 1999-2003 programming cycle. the United Nations 
system in Kenya. in collaboration with its partners, has cstablishcd eleven inter-agency thematic 
working groups (each coordinated by the Representative of a United Nations agency). This process 
resulted in the following three broad strategic objectives with a number of theme groups established 
for each (lead agencies indicated in parentheses): 
• Strategic Objective One - To accelerate sustainable economic growth for poveny reduction. 
Theme groups on: industrialisation and emplo~ent generation (UNIDO); food security and 
rural development (FAO); and natural resource management (FAO). 
• Strategic Objective Two - To expand access to and quality of basic social services. Theme 
groups on: education ( UNICEF); health and nutrition (WHO); water and sanitation 
(UNICEF); and population and developmcnt strategics (UNFPA). 
• Strategic Objective Three • To foster an enabling environment for sustainable human 
development. Theme groups on: economics and govemance (UNDP); disaster management 
(WFP): gender (UNIFEM): and HlV/AIDS prevention and care {UNAIDS). 
6. In addition. inter-ag,ncy coordinating committees have been established in three arcas: 
Administration and Operations (coordinated by UNDP/UNON); Infonnation and Communication 
(coordinated by UNIC) and Security (Office of the Resident Coordinator). These groups will allow the 
United Nations to move forward in its attempts to improve coordination t,etween the United Nations 
family especially in budgeting, disbursement. accounting procedüres and standardisation of programme planning and management. This will have positive impacts on the United Nations· 
relationship with Government and other partners. 
7. The United Nations system in Kenya is managed through the Resident Coordinator System led 
by the U nited Nations Resident Coordinator under the guidance and advice of the KCC The Resident 
Coordinator System is supported by a Secretariat anda Technical Committee, which serve to enhance 
and monitor United Nations coordination and collaboration through the mechanisms set forth in che 
UNDAF. 
8. A United Nations Common Resource Framework for Kenya has also been established with an 
estimated $390,000,000 of development assistance to be mobilised during the 1999 - 2003 
programming cycle. 
2. INTRODUCTION 
9. The development challenges faced by Kenya have been identified in the Govemment of 
Kenya·s Country Strategy Note (CSN) of 1994 and the United Nations Common Country Assessment 
(CCA). The Govemment of Kenya (GoK) has outlined it's strategies in the Eighty Nacional 
Development Plan and various sessional and policy framework papers which cover a broad range of 
interventions on national development issues. The Government is committed to the improvement of 
the well being and quality of life of the individual. the family, and the nation as a whole through the 
development and implementation of appropriate policies. strategíes and programmes. 
1 O. Past efforts by the Government together with its intemational development partners to tackle 
poverty in Kenya have largely been unsuccessful. as development gains have tended to benefit those 
who already have adequate resources. Lessons leamed from programme implementation indicate that 
more attention should. in the future. be paid to the effects of poverty on the attainment of human 
development targets. Furthermore. the protection of the most vulnerable groups through a strong 
emphasis on children ·s rights as well as empowerment of women and communities. is a prerequisite 
for sustainable development. 
11. The Cnited Nations Development Assistance Framework process is the United Nations 
response to development challenges faced by Kenya which aims to promote collaboration and 
collective efficiency among United Nations agencies to support the Govemment of Kenya in reaching 
it' s national development goals. The consolidation of country level programming under one enhanced 
L'nited Nations Resident Coordinator Svstem is one of the Secretarv-General's United Nations reform 
initiatives. With this approach. the lFÑDP Resident Representativ~ also serves as the L'nited Nations 
System Resident Coordinator. The UNDAF process is being piloted in 18 countries. starting with 1 1 
c0untries in 1997 and an additional seven in 1998. Kenya is one of the 18 UNDAF pilot countries. 
I he UNDAF process builds on the Common Country Assessment through a series of systematic steps. 
12. A Common Country Assessment (CCA) was completed in March 1998. The CCA gives an 
overview of the development status in Kenya. using a broad range of social and economic indicators. 
As a result of the CCA process. the KCC was able to identify key areas of need for development 
collaboration. as well as indicators to measure progress towards reaching global and national 
development goals. The CCA served as the first step towards the UNDAF consolidation and 
rationalisation of U nitcd Nations development assistance. 
13. In February 1998. the first UNDAF preparatory meeting was held with ali heads of agencies at 
the KCC .-\nnual Retreat. The process and content areas of UNDAF were discussed. UNDAF 
facilitator inputs we!'e received. anda list of agency concerns generated. The KCC forrnulated its first 
inter-agency miss ion statement. strategic objectives. and thematic focus areas for the period 1999-
2003. Based on the UNOAF provisional guidelines, an UNDAF workplan was agreed upon. This 
initial UNDAF outlíne also served as the basis for the 1998 Resident Coordinator system workplan. 14. Toe KCC identified three overall strategic objectives for its assistance to Kenya. and 
established eleven theme groups to address Kcnya's most urgent development concems and to followup on agreements reached in key areas of global conferences and conventions. Theme groups and 
operations committees met to develop five-year strategies as welJ as 1999 work plans with activiry 
clusters and indicators for measuring progress towards realising human development targets. (Annexes 
A, B &. C). 
15. Following the KCC's commitment to the UNDAF process, Toe Resident Coordinator had 
consultations with the Ministry of Planning and National Development, the Ministry of Finance. the 
Office of the President, the donor community (Kenya Coordination Group), the Federation of Kenya 
Employers, and the National Council of Non-Govemmental Organisations. In addition, Govemment. 
donor, and NGO/civil society outrcach prcsentations of the UNDAF took place in the latter part of 
1998. 
3. DEVELORMENT CHALLENGES IN KENYA 
3.1 Humall Development Cballeages and National Priorities 
"Human Poverty is more than income poverty - it is the denial o/ choices and opportunities for living 
a tolerable lije". Human Development Report. 1997 (UNDP) 
3.1.1 Background 
16. In its National Development plans, the GoK has identified the country's overriding 
development challenges to be alleviation of poverty, eradication of illiteracy and disease. and the 
creation of employment through high sustained economic growth. An estimated 12.6 million (or 43.4 
per cent) of Kenya's total population of 29 million live in absolute poverty. In its 1996-1998 Policy 
Framework Paper on economic reforms, the GoK recognised that a minimum of 6 per cent annual 
GDP growth is required to achieve significant reductions in unemployment and poverty. The GDP 
grov,th rate in 1997 was estimated at 2. 9 per cent. 
17. Economic development in Kenya. which largely depends on exploitation of the country" s 
natural resources, is currently unsustainable, as many of these resources cannot sustain present rates of 
utilisation. Poor perfonnance in the key sectors of agriculture, manufacturing, and tourism prohibits 
the achievement of the overall GDP target growth rate of 6 per cent per annum necessary to provide 
subsistence requirements, generate adequate employment and foreign exchange eamings. and alleviate 
poverty. 
18. Overall, the quality and coverage of social services have deteriorated in the last ten years. 
Apart from literacy levels, Kenya is far from achieving intemational and national goals aimed at 
meeting the basic needs ofthe population despite reaffirtning its commitment to improving the welfare 
of ali Kenyans, particularly of children and women. Kenya has endorsed conclusion of the World 
1 Summit for Children ( 1990), World Conference on Education For Ali (l 990), lntemational 
Conference on Nutrition (1992), United Nations Conference on Environment and Development 
( 1992 ), World Conference on Human Rights ( 1993 ), lntematíonal Conference on Population and 
Develop.,.ent ( 1994), World Summit for Social Oevelopment (1995), the Founh World Conference on 
Women (1995) Second UN Conference on Human Settlements (1996), World Food Swnmit (1996). 
Kenya has also ratitied the 1979 Convention on the Elimination of all Fonns of Discrimination against 
Women (CEDAW) and the Convention of the Rights ofthe Child (1989). 
19. Regional and gcnder disparitics in accessing basic services as well as in representation in 
political and economic decision-making are clearly evident in the country. This is mainly due to 
differences in resource endowment and accessibility. In additíon factors such as widespread poverty 
and traditional cultural practices exacerbate the problem. Glaring disparities are in areas such as girls · education; in the leve( of poverty among female-headed households; and in the legal provisions for 
women, e.g. inheritance laws and laws for protection and empowerment. 
20. Based on its discussions, and aided by the Common Country Assessment (CCA), the United 
Nations Kenya Country Committee (KCC) agreed on a number of priority areas for cooperation. The 
KCC agreed on a common United Nations system mission statement, and identified the following 
three strategic areas of collaborative intervention for the 1999-2003 programming cycle: la) 
accelerating sustainable economic growth for poverty reduction; (b) expanding access to and 
irnproving quality ofbasic social services: and (c) promoting an enabling environment for sustainable 
human development. UNDAF becomes the document within which individual agencies and 
programmes address these priority areas using the common programming strategies identified. 
3.1.2 Accelerating Sustainable Economic Growtb for Poverty Reduction 
lndustrialisatioa and Employment Generation 
21. The Govemment view is that unemployment and poverty are the twin challenges of Kenya's 
development process. With an estimated 12.6 million Kenyans living below the poverty line and 
almost 3 million unemployed, the Govemment sees industrialisation as an effective avenue for the 
generation of adequate employment opportunities and higher incomes. Although a key sector of the 
economy, agriculture has limited potential to generate the accelerated growth needed in employment 
and income generation. 
22. A key element in the GoK's economic strategy is to focus on the development ofthe industrial 
sector as a means of accelerating the growth rate of the economy so as to substantially increase per 
capita income and generate sufficient employment for the rapidly growing labour force. Projected 
growth rates for both employment and manufacturing as outlined in the Eighth National Development 
Plan and Sessional Paper No. 2 ( 1997) have thus far not been achieved. Total employment is expected 
to grow atan annual rate of 3.5 per cent. The most promising employment opportunities are expected 
in the informal sector where employment is expected to grow at the rate of 6.5 per cent per annum. 
23. The Eighth '.'/ational Development Plan (NDP), unlike previous development plans. addresses 
one significant sectoral issue - industrialisation. The theme of the NDP is rapid industrialisation for 
sustained development. The NDP is intended to lay the foundation for the transfonnation of Kenya's 
economy by the year 20:?0 to that of a country with the status of a newly industrialised country. The 
purpose of the Sessional Paper is to provide a framework of Govemment policies that will stimulate 
economic growth and employment through the expansion ofthe industrial sector. 
2-l. The Govemment's industrial development strategy is a means to generate and sustain the GDP 
and employrnent target rates. lncluded in this strateg)' is the promotion of the small enterprise and "jua 
kali" sectors. Sessional Paper No. 2 of 1992 provides the policy framework for promoting such 
enterprises. The creation of productive employment. according to Sessional Paper No. 2 of 1997. is 
the major imperative for industrialisation. 
25. Departing from its past interventionist I strategy, che Govemment will concentrate on che 
provision of an enabling environment in which the prívate sector is expected to help generate the 
above opportunities. A conducive business environment will include the provision and maintenance of 
infrastructure. comprehensíve and efficient support services. and the assurance of a stable supply of 
skilled labour. A key aim will be to design a manpower training system that will ease transition from 
education and training institutions to work at ali levels through a focus on the provision of appropriate 
training. Job training will be emphasised and measures will be taken to cater for the special needs of 
industry. 26. The Govemment also emphasises the need to enter into dialogue with private sector and local 
communities in order to identify, formulate and implement relevant industrialisation policies. 
strategies and programmes. To this end, the NDP calls for the establishment of a National lndustrial 
Oevelopment Council. 
27. The United Nations system goal and objectives for industrialisation and employment 
assistance to Kenya. the United Nations system activities, impact indicators, and Theme Group partner 
agencies are indicated in Annex A-1 and Annex C. 
Food Security and Rural Development 
28. As recognised by the World Food Summit Plan of Action, food security and poverty 
eradication are intimately linked. The Declaration and Plan of Action give Govemments the prime 
responsibility for achieving food security and outline effective policies and strategies to make 
sustainable progress towardf the elimination of hunger and malnutrition in order to achieve sustainable 
development. 
29. The agricultura! sector provídes the bulk of Kenya's staple foods. Eighty four per cent of 
farmland in Kenya is used for local food products. The 1994 Sessional Paper No. 2 on National Food 
Policy and the current Country Strategy Note recognise that food security should have top priority 
since no meaningful development in economic, social or cultural spheres is possible without it. 
30. The Government gives high priority to poverty alleviation and improved household and 
national food security. Household food security is influenced by cultural factors, access to family 
resources by ali its members and coping mechanisms, among other factors. National food security is 
limited by severe budgetary constraints, which makes replenishment of food resources dífficult. 
31. Poverty is overwhelmingly rural. lt is estimated that 47 per cent of rural and 29 per cent of 
urban Kenyans were food poor in 1994. The highest leve Is of food poverty were found in Eastern ( 60 
per cent). North Eastern (57 per cent) and Western (52 per cent) provinces. However. overall food 
poverty levels declined from 1982 to 1994. particularly in Nyanza (from 77 per cent to 40 per cent). 
32. Eradicating poverty must necessarily address the central issue of encouraging the groMh of 
economic opportunities for the rural poor on their farms and in their enterprises, and of women in 
particular. Around 80 per cent of the population are rural, of which 47 per cent are poor. The 
agricultura( sector accounts for 26 per cent of the GDP, 80 per cent of national employment (51 per 
cent by small holders ), 60 per cent of export earnings. and 45 per cent of Government revenue. Given 
these numbers, national income and employment growth t~rgets are not likely to be achieved without a 
growing rural economy. 
33. One of Kenya's national goals is to achieve food self-sufficiency in major staples. such as 
maize. by 2010 which in tum will contribute to sustainable economic development and poverty 
oeradication. National priorities include improved efficiency and effectiveness of govemment services 
in agriculture. enhancement of rural social capital/community participation. increased agricultura! 
productivity and farm family income. and enhanced economic opportunitics for the rural poor. 
34. Significant investments and policy changes have taken place in the agricultural sector 
(building an impressive research system, liberalising agricultura! markets. etc.) but these have tended 
to benefit those most able to take advantage of the new opportunities. Cereal production per capita is 
down to about half of what it was 20 years ago, for example, with almost 40% of the population 
chronically undernourished. 
35. Loessons leamed from previous experience show that there has been good diagnosis but weak 
implementation of remedies. There has been a policy gap between broad national plans and routine sector actions and projects, while decentralised and crosscutting programmes continue to face 
problems of limited resources and weak commitment of sector staff and systems. 
36. The United Nations system goal and objectives for food security and ruraJ development 
assistance, the cluster of United Nations system activities. impact indicators and Theme Group partner 
agencies are indicated in Annex A-2 and Annex C. 
Natural Resource Management 
37. ln Kenya. serious environmental problems have adversely impacted upon the socio-economic 
development of the country. These problems suggest the need for greatly improved natural resource 
management. Nearly 80 per cent of the country is arid or semi-arid and vulnerable to increased 
desertification. According to the National Environmental Action Plan (NEAP), priority problems 
include: degradation of soil and water resources; increased deforestation amid growing fuelwood 
demand: growing contlicts over coastal and marine resources that relate to tourism: and urban waste 
management and pollution from transportation, among others. 
38. Kenya has ratified a number of global environmental conventions, including the Convention 
on Bio-diversity, the Convention to Combat Desertification, the Convention on Climate Change, the 
Convention on Intemational Trade in Endangered Species of wild fauna and flora. the Ramsar 
Convention on Wetlands and the Conventinn on the conservation of Migratory Species of wild 
animals. 
39. The Govemment's commitrnent to conservation and sustainable use of natural resources has 
been stated in all its eight national development plans. Kenya·s environmental policy is based on the 
following broad objectives: 
• to facilitate optima! use of land and water resources in improving the quality of the human 
environment; 
• to promote sustainable use of natural resources to meet the needs of present and füture 
generations: 
• to treat environmental conservation and economic development as integral aspects of the same 
process of sustainable development; and 
• to conserve bio-diversity, to reverse desertification. to mitigate effects of disasters. and to 
maintain an ecological balance. 
-10. Current development efforts emphasise production with linle regard for environmental 
conservarion, while convemional environmemal conservatjon ad1,ocates resource protection. Thc 
country possesses an estimated 35.000 known species of animals. plants and micro-organisms. These 
resources are increasingly under pressure from unsustainable use. resulting in air, water, soil pollution. 
,oil erosion and depletion.

3.1.J Expanding Access to and Improving Quality of Basic Social Ser-vices 
Education 
:?. Education as a fundamental right for all was first indicated by the World Conference on 
Education for Ali ( 1990) and by the World Summit on Children { 1990). Toe Fourth World Conference on Women (Beijing 1995) emphasised that women and girls should be provided with increased access 
to education and advocated the promotion of measures to eradicate poverty through education. 
43. As with other social services, lack of access to education in Kenya mainly affects the poor. A 
number of national goals were established in 1992 in Kenya's Programme of Action for Children. 
However, perfonnance in the education sector remains poor and this can be attributed to a range of 
factors: (i) high poverty levels, coupled with the increasing cost of education (ii) lack of facilities . 
especially for post-primary education; and (iii) socio-cultural aspects, particularly affecting enrolment 
of girls. 
44. The World Summit for Children set a global target of achieving 85 per cent literacy by the 
year 2000. Although Kenya's target for the same year is 80 per cent. large disparities exist along 
regional and gender lines. Regional disparities exist at all levels of education - from primary to 
university with North Eastem Province having particularly low enrolment rates compared to other 
provinces. North Eastem Province has an exceptionally low literacy rate of24 per cent. 
45. Gender disparities are more apparent in secondary than in primary education, 24.5 per cent 
girl's enrolmeqt in 1996 against 28.4 for boys. Most provinces demonstrate literacy rates above 50 per 
cent for both males and females. In 1994, the overall female literacy rate was 67 per cent compared to 
83 per cent for males. Ali provinces showed gender disparities, with the greatest gaps occurring in 
North Eastem, Coast and Nyanza, and the lowest being Nairobi and Central Provinces . 
.t6. The GoK has projected that participation rates for early childhood education should increase 
from the current level of 30 per cent to 50 per cent. However, gross enrolment rates (GER) in preprimary schools have been low, rising marginally from 34.7 per cent in 1989 to 35.7 per cent in 1996. 
The GER far primary schools has declined steadily from 95 per cent in 1989 to 78 per cent in l 996. 
Enrolment trends for secondary schools showed a similar declining trend with rates falling from 31 per 
cent in 1989 to 26.5 per cent in 1996. 
-l7. The Govemment of Kenya's goal is to achieve universal primary education for ali children by 
the year 2000. As of now. gross enrolment rates (GER) in pre-primary schools, primary schools. and 
secondary schools ali fall below the national targets. This poor perfonnance in the education sector 
could impact negatively on the achievements of the national goal of becoming a newly industrialised 
country by 2020. 
-l8. The Govemrnent has prepared a Master Plan on Education and Training for Kenya· s 
industrialisation in the year 2020 which will be used as a reference for educational development in the 
country.

51. The Primary Health Care Conference in Alma Ata in 1978 (organised by WHO and UNICEF) 
set the stage for increased access to health care for vulnerable groups and has become a tuming point 
for universal health care. Kenya has adopted this approach in the restructuring of its health services by 
promoting district health system support for operationalizing the PHC approach. 
52. In Kenya, problems have been encountered in drug shortages, dilapidating infrastructure. high 
tumover of health workers. lack of adequate mechanisms for epidemic detection and control. 
increasing resistance of malaria to cheap and easily available drugs and high HIV/AIDS prevalence 
rates reversing the trend in the control of tuberculosis. The response of the Govemment has been a 
plan to refonn the health sector. This plan has the backing of all stakeholders and is already ongoing. 
The World Food Conference in 1974 established that every human being has the right to be free from 
hunger and under-nutrition in order to develop their physical and mental faculties. The World Summit 
for Children ( 1990) set a rarget to reduce moderate and severe under-nutrition among the under-five to 
halfthe 1990 level by the year 2000. The FAO World Food Summit of 1996 set a goal ofhalving the 
incidence of under-nutrition by the year 20 l S. 
53. Major priorities for action are child survival, safe motherhood, disease and malnutrition 
control, HIV/AIDS prevention, control of epidemics and the realisation of household food security. 
Poverty reduction, equity in service provision, mitigation against the adverse effects associated with 
emergency, enhancement of cost sharing, decentralisation in both public and prívate health and 
nutrition services will be addressed in the Govemment's strategic imperatives. The health and nutrition 
challenges are being addressed in Kenya and although the Govemment has taken a prominent role. it 
has also bccomc evident that the Govemment's resources for financing health careare inadequate to
